## Solution

**Answer:** The limit is $\dfrac{5}{6}$.

**Proof.**

Set up a probability space with i.i.d. random variables $X_1, X_2, \ldots \sim \mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$. The given integral equals

$$I_n \;=\; \mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^5}{\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^4}\right].$$

**Step 1: Almost-sure convergence of the ratio.**

Define $S_k^{(n)}=\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k$. For $X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(0,1)$,

$$\mathbb{E}[X^4]=\int_0^1 x^4\,dx=\frac15, \qquad \mathbb{E}[X^5]=\int_0^1 x^5\,dx=\frac16.$$

By the Strong Law of Large Numbers,

$$\frac{S_4^{(n)}}{n}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\frac15, \qquad \frac{S_5^{(n)}}{n}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\frac16.$$

Since $P(S_4^{(n)}=0)=P(X_1=\cdots=X_n=0)=0$, the ratio is well-defined a.s., and

$$\frac{S_5^{(n)}}{S_4^{(n)}}=\frac{S_5^{(n)}/n}{S_4^{(n)}/n}\xrightarrow{\text{a.s.}}\frac{1/6}{1/5}=\frac56.$$

**Step 2: Uniform integrability / domination.**

For $x\in[0,1]$ we have $x^5\le x^4$, so $0\le S_5^{(n)}\le S_4^{(n)}$, hence

$$0\le \frac{S_5^{(n)}}{S_4^{(n)}}\le 1.$$

The ratio is bounded by the constant $1$, which is integrable on the probability space.

**Step 3: Apply the Dominated Convergence Theorem.**

By the DCT,

$$\lim_{n\to\infty} I_n=\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac{S_5^{(n)}}{S_4^{(n)}}\right]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\frac56\right]=\frac56.$$

Therefore,

$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \int_{[0,1]^n} \frac{x_1^5 + \cdots + x_n^5}{x_1^4 + \cdots + x_n^4}\,dx_1\cdots dx_n = \frac{5}{6}.$$
